source.authorsText:
This sky culture was initially contributed by *Karrie Berglund* of Digitalis Education Solutions, Inc. based on Hong Kong Space Museum star maps (no longer available online).

Sun Shuwei [sunshuwei.hi@foxmail.com](mailto:sunshuwei.hi@foxmail.com) replenishes more than 200 Xingguans and more than 3,000 stars, based primarily on the book *Chinese and Western Contrast Star Chart and Catalogue 1950.0* by Yi Shitong, and add the description.

**Statement**: The basic reference for the cultural map of China's sky cultures is Tan Qixiang's *Historical Atlas of China* (中国历史地图集). It does not reflect any modern borders, nor does it reflect the political intentions of the artist, and is for reference only. The boundaries shown on the map have been significantly simplified and only indicate general outlines, without reflecting any detailed demarcation. The cartographer does not guarantee the accuracy of these boundaries, and any improvements with better delineations are welcome.

source.authorsText: This Greco-Egyptian sky culture was painted and added to Stellarium by: _Susanne M. Hoffmann: service@uhura-uraniae.com _ Written in English: _SMH_ ### About This sky culture is a mapping of historical figures onto the stars. The figures are directly copied by hand from the digital photographs that are provided by the Louvre and the colours follow roughly the reconstruction by Alexandre N.Isis (wikicommons, 2013). ### Acknowledgements We thank Christian Leitz, Daniela Mendel-Leitz and Andreas Winkler for interesting exchange about this artifact, Daniela Mendel-Leitz specifically for her guidance in Dendera's temple. The collaboration with Juan Belmonte has been a pleasure and its continuation might lead to more results in the future. Youla Azkarrula assisted technologically. ### Fair Use This sky culture originates from research. We provide this for free but the authors of contributions certainly deserve to be cited according to the common rules. Thank you!

This sky culture was contributed to Stellarium by Jakob Eyermann consulting with Susanne M. Hoffmann as part of a German studies term paper.

### About

Sophie Marshall and Susanne M. Hoffmann served as mentors during the research process. Several constellations were taken from the Rimtöl gloss and thus from Jonas Persson's sky culture “Norse”.

traditions.label: Hebrew (biblical names)

unlocated.name: ʿAsh / ʿAyish
unlocated.notes: Job 9:9 names Ash; Job 38:32 names Ayish with its children. traditions.label: Hebrew (medieval zodiac)
traditions.description: Twelve attested Hebrew zodiac names on modern reference outlines, kept separate from the biblical-name layer.
traditions.historicalScope: Medieval Hebrew astronomical naming, documented in Maimonides (12th century); corroborated by a Sefer Yetzirah recension.
traditions.geometryNotice: Names follow the medieval Hebrew sources. Connecting lines use modern Stellarium figures; medieval zodiac calculations use twelve equal 30° divisions.

traditions.label: Zoroastrian (Avestan names)
traditions.description: Three securely identified stellar names shown with unconnected reference markers; Vanant and Satavaēsa remain unplotted candidates.
traditions.period: Younger Avestan textual tradition; date of composition not fixed by this layer.
traditions.geometryNotice: Rings mark modern reference stars. The cited Avestan texts give names and descriptions, without connecting lines.

source.authors: Mazzaroth project; Avestan text after Geldner; astronomical identifications discussed by D. N. MacKenzie and Antonio Panaino

source.changes: Selected three supported object identifications. Modern catalogue members serve only as unconnected locators; no connecting lines or hypothetical outlines were reconstructed.

constellations.name: Tištrya · Sirius
constellations.evidence: Named in Yašt 8; Panaino identifies the star with Sirius.
constellations.notes: The ring locates Sirius itself. This is a stellar identification, not a constellation outline.

sources.label: Yašt 8.1–3 and 8.12
Antonio Panaino, Tištrya, Encyclopaedia Iranica (2005)

constellations.name: Haptōiringa · Great Bear
constellations.evidence: Yašt 8.12 names Haptōiringa; Iranian studies identify it with the Great Bear.
constellations.notes: Seven Big Dipper stars are modern reference members for the attested seven-star group.

sources.label: Yašt 8.12
Antonio Panaino, Haftōrang, Encyclopaedia Iranica (2002)

constellations.name: Paoiryaēinyas · Pleiades
constellations.evidence: Yašt 8.12 preserves the name; MacKenzie identifies the group as the Pleiades.
constellations.notes: The atlas’s nine catalogue reference members locate the cluster. This display choice does not assert an ancient Iranian count of nine stars.

sources.label: Yašt 8.12
D. N. MacKenzie, Constellations, Encyclopaedia Iranica (1992)

unlocated.name: Vanant
unlocated.evidence: Named in Yašt 8.12; Vega is used in modern Iranian studies.
unlocated.notes: Several historical identifications have been proposed for Vanant. Its relationship to the later Bundahishn stellar chiefs is uncertain.

sources.label: Yašt 8.12
Encyclopaedia Iranica, Mithra i., discussion of Vanant (Yašt 21.1)

unlocated.name: Satavaēsa
unlocated.evidence: Yašt 8.0 and 8.9 name the astral collaborator of Tištrya; Panaino calls the Fomalhaut identification probable.
unlocated.notes: Its identification is uncertain. Later stellar-chief lists and translations give differing interpretations.

sources.label: Yašt 8.0 and 8.9
Antonio Panaino, Tištrya, Encyclopaedia Iranica (2005)
